key_terms.meaning: Machine driven by the engine or APU that converts mechanical power into electrical power at a controlled voltage and frequency
A thick copper bar that collects generator output and feeds it to many load circuits through individual protection
GCU functions that trip the generator circuit breaker and remove the field when output leaves its band; over-voltage fast and inverse-time, under-voltage time-delayed
Transformer plus rectifier that steps 115 V AC down and converts it to 28 V DC
Device that converts DC into AC at the frequency the load needs, e.g. 28 V DC to 115 V AC 400 Hz
Single-winding transformer with a tapped winding that raises or lowers AC voltage with little loss
Alkaline cell, about 1.2 V per cell, with low internal resistance and high discharge current, standard for engine starting and emergency DC
Small air-driven turbine that drops into the slipstream and spins a generator when all main power is lost
Generator with a fixed magnet rotor; needs no field supply, so it survives loss of all DC and feeds essential AC
Extended-range twin-engine operations: rules that fix how far a twin may fly from an alternate airport, sized by emergency power and time available
Exterior red (left), green (right) and white (tail) lights that show the aircraft's heading to other traffic at night
Standard case size, connector layout and mounting for avionics boxes, so boxes from different makers interchange
Electromagnetic interference is unwanted coupling into a circuit; electromagnetic compatibility is the ability to work beside other equipment without either disturbing the other
Instrument that reads the difference between total pressure and static pressure, and displays it as speed
Instrument that reads static pressure alone and displays height above a set pressure datum
Temperature of the gas leaving the engine, measured by thermocouples; a direct check on turbine health and thrust
Voltage regulator that varies field current by squeezing a stack of carbon discs, whose resistance falls as pressure rises
Slow-blow fuse-like device that carries normal current indefinitely but opens on a heavy sustained fault
Bus arrangement where generators run in parallel on the ground or when needed, but feed separate halves in flight so one fault stays local
AC whose frequency follows engine speed instead of being fixed at 400 Hz; loads must accept the wider band
Tank probes plus a computer that convert capacitance or resistance changes into fuel mass or volume in the cockpit

takeaways: A generator is only useful once its voltage is regulated, its output is switched to a busbar, and its faults are cleared before wiring overheats.
Converters exist because different loads need different forms of power: 115 V AC 400 Hz, 28 V DC, and on newer aircraft 235 V AC variable frequency and 270 V DC.
The battery starts the engine or APU and bridges the gap between losing all generators and getting another source online.
The ram air turbine and the permanent magnet generator are the last line of defence, and ETOPS rules decide how much time that line must buy.
Aircraft lights divide by user (crew, cabin, outside world), and each group gets its own supply, control and failure requirement.
An avionics box must be packaged to a standard form, cooled by a defined path, and designed to meet interference limits, or it will not be fitted to an aircraft.
The airspeed indicator reads total minus static pressure; the altimeter reads static pressure alone.
Voltage regulators all do one thing: compare output with a reference and move field current to close the gap.
Protection is chosen from the derated rating of the wire, not from the load current, otherwise the wire becomes the fuse.
Bus architecture decides how much aircraft is lost when one generator or one bus fails.
bank_note: Most syllabi examine this unit through long answers that follow the power from source to load: generation and regulation, conversion, batteries and emergency power, distribution and bus systems, protection, and the A320 and B787 architectures. Questions on regulators, circuit protection and bus systems usually include a calculation.

bank.q: Explain how a generator's output reaches an aircraft load. Cover the generator control unit, the generator circuit breaker, the busbar, and over-voltage and under-voltage protection.
outline: Generator, GCB, busbar, load breaker, load: the power path
GCU beside the path: regulates field, senses, trips
GCB closes only when the output is inside limits
Over-voltage: fast inverse-time trip and field removal
Under-voltage: time-delayed trip so motor-start dips ride through
Each load fed through its own breaker
answer: Name the power path. On an AC transport aircraft the generator (an IDG at 115 V, 400 Hz, or a variable-frequency generator) feeds its generator circuit breaker (GCB), the GCB feeds the main AC busbar, and the busbar feeds each load through that load's own circuit breaker. A DC channel is the same with a reverse-current cut-out in place of the GCB. Draw it as a straight line: generator → GCB → busbar → load breaker → load.

Place the control block. The generator control unit (GCU) is not in the power path and carries no load current. It senses generator voltage, current and frequency, controls the field current to hold the voltage at 115 V (or 28 V on a DC system), and commands the GCB to close or trip. Draw it to the side with a field-control line to the generator and a trip line to the GCB.

Explain the busbar. The busbar is a thick copper or aluminium bar that collects the generator output and shares it among many load circuits. Its resistance is kept low so the voltage at every load is nearly the bus voltage. Grouping loads on buses (main, essential, battery) lets protection drop a group without losing the rest.

State when the GCB closes. The GCU closes the GCB only when the generator voltage and frequency are inside their normal band, so a generator that has not built up, or is out of limits, is never connected. MIL-STD-704 sets the normal steady-state band at the equipment as 108 to 118 V for a 115 V AC system and 22 to 29 V for a 28 V DC system.

Explain over-voltage protection. A runaway field (for example a failed regulator driving full field) can push the bus far above its band within a fraction of a second, damaging insulation and every connected load. The over-voltage unit therefore trips fast and on an inverse-time curve: the higher the excess, the quicker the trip. The GCU removes the field and opens the GCB together, because opening the GCB alone leaves an excited machine.

Explain under-voltage protection. A generator whose voltage sags (a weak field, a drive fault, an overload) would drag the bus down and starve the loads. The under-voltage trip opens the GCB, but only after a time delay, so a short dip while a large motor starts does not drop the generator. The bus then transfers to another source through the bus tie.

Add the other protections briefly: over-current and differential (stator or feeder fault) trip the GCB at once; under- and over-frequency trips the GCB on an AC system; a seized IDG drive is cleared by the mechanical drive disconnect, not by an electrical trip.

answer.text: Summarise the actions in a table.

head: Fault
What it endangers
Action
rows: Fast inverse-time trip; field off and GCB open

answer: Close with the load end: each load breaker protects that load's wire, so a short in one lamp circuit opens only its breaker and the bus stays up. Check: in the power path, only the GCB and the load breakers carry generator current; the GCU never does.

bank.q: Compare lead-acid, nickel-cadmium and lithium-ion aircraft batteries: construction, cell voltage, number of cells in a 24 V battery, charging and the main hazard of each. A 40 Ah battery supplies 40 A for 30 minutes: find the depth of discharge.
outline: Lead-acid: PbO₂ and Pb plates, sulphuric acid, about 2 V per cell, 12 cells
NiCd: nickel hydroxide and cadmium plates, KOH, about 1.2 V, 19 or 20 cells
Lithium-ion: 3.6 to 3.7 V per cell, eight cells, BMS required
Charging: CC then CV for lead-acid; CC with cut-offs for NiCd; BMS-controlled for lithium
Hazards: sulphation and acid; thermal runaway on CV charge; cell runaway and fire
answer: Lead-acid construction: positive plates of lead dioxide, negative plates of sponge lead, electrolyte of dilute sulphuric acid. Each cell is about 2.1 V on open circuit and about 2 V on load, so a 24 V battery has 12 cells. Specific gravity near 1.28 shows full charge, because charging raises the acid strength.

Nickel-cadmium construction: positive plates of nickel hydroxide and negative plates of cadmium, usually sintered into a porous nickel matrix, in potassium hydroxide electrolyte. Each cell is about 1.2 V, so a 24 V battery has 20 cells (24 V) or 19 cells (about 22.8 V). The electrolyte does not take part in the reaction, so specific gravity does not show the state of charge.

Lithium-ion construction: a lithium metal-oxide (or iron-phosphate) positive electrode and a graphite negative in an organic electrolyte. Each cell is about 3.6 to 3.7 V, so only about eight cells are needed; the B787 main and APU batteries are eight-cell lithium-ion units.

answer.text: Put the comparison in a table.

head: Property
Lead-acid
NiCd
Lithium-ion
rows: CC with voltage and temperature cut-off
BMS per cell, CC then CV with cut-off

answer: Explain the NiCd hazard: on a constant-voltage charge a warm cell's voltage falls, so the charger pushes more current, which heats the cell further; the loop runs away until electrolyte boils off or a cell vents. Aircraft NiCd chargers therefore charge at constant current and stop on voltage or temperature, and the battery carries temperature sensors.

Explain the lithium hazard: an overcharged, over-discharged or damaged cell can go into thermal runaway and ignite its neighbours. Every lithium battery needs a battery management system that watches each cell voltage and temperature, balances the cells and cuts the charge. After the two B787 battery events of January 2013 the fleet was grounded for about three months, and the fix added cell insulation, a steel case and an overboard vent.
State a strength of each: lead-acid is cheap and simple; NiCd gives very high current for engine starts, works well in cold and has a long life; lithium-ion gives the most energy for its weight.

answer.pre:
Ah used   = I × t = 40 A × 0.5 h = 20 Ah
DoD       = 20 Ah ÷ 40 Ah × 100 = 50 %
remaining = 40 − 20 = 20 Ah

answer: Check: 40 A from a 40 Ah battery is the 1-hour (1C) rate, so half an hour must remove half the capacity, 50 %, which agrees. At this high rate the usable capacity is a little below 40 Ah, so the real remaining charge is slightly less than 20 Ah.

bank.q: Describe the flight-compartment, cabin and exterior lighting of a transport aircraft, stating the supply and control of each group. An emergency lighting pack of 24 V, 4 Ah and 6 A maximum feeds 12 exit signs of 6 W and 20 floor lights of 3 W for 12 minutes: does it hold?
outline: Flight compartment: flood, integral panel, chart, dome, standby lights; dimmed
Cabin: ceiling, sidewall, reading, signs; split across buses
Emergency: exit signs, floor-proximity, escape lights on own packs
Exterior: navigation red/green/white with arcs, beacon and strobes, landing, taxi, logo, wing scan
Dimming: rheostat or PWM
Pack: 132 W, 5.5 A, 1.1 Ah, holds
answer: Flight compartment lights: flood lights wash the whole panel; integral panel lights are built into the panels and back-light the engraved legends; a chart light is a focused swivel lamp; a dome light gives general white light; a standby light on its own battery means the crew is never in total darkness. Supply: mostly 28 V DC (integral lighting is often 5 V or 28 V, older types 26 V AC from an auto-transformer). Control: dimmers on the overhead and glareshield panels, by rheostat or pulse-width control; pulse-width dimming wastes almost no power and does not shift the colour.

Cabin lights: ceiling and sidewall lights along the tube, reading lights in each passenger service unit, galley and lavatory lights, and the illuminated signs. Supply: AC or DC buses, deliberately split across buses so one bus failure darkens only part of the cabin. Control: the cabin lighting panel at the attendant station switches groups and sets brightness.

Emergency (egress) lights: exit signs at each door, floor-proximity strips along the aisle, and escape lights that light the slides or the overwing area. Supply: self-contained battery packs that float on an essential bus and take over when that bus fails; rules ask for at least 10 minutes. Control: an arming switch in the cockpit and a switch at the attendant station.

Exterior lights: navigation (position) lights, red on the left wingtip through 110°, green on the right through 110°, white at the tail through 140°; anti-collision lights, a red beacon on top and bottom of the fuselage plus white wingtip strobes, switched on before engine start; landing lights in the wing root or on the nose gear, taxi and runway turn-off lights, logo lights on the tail, and wing scan lights for ice inspection. Supply: 28 V DC or AC by type; landing lights are the largest lighting loads, a 600 W lamp on 28 V drawing 21.4 A.

answer.text: Solve the pack question step by step.

answer: Conclude: the pack holds. The current, 5.5 A, is inside the 6 A limit, and 12 minutes uses only 27.5 % of the capacity. Endurance at this load is at most 4 ÷ 5.5 = 0.727 h, 43.6 minutes; the real figure is lower because capacity falls at high current, but it is still well over 12 minutes.
Check: two separate limits were tested, current (A) and charge (Ah). A pack can fail on current even when it has charge to spare, so both must be stated in the answer.

bank.q: Explain the construction and working of a vibrating-contact voltage regulator and state its drawbacks. A 28 V generator has a field resistance of 8 Ω and the regulator inserts 16 Ω when its contact opens; the field needs an average of 2.0 A. Find the duty cycle.
outline: Voltage coil across the output, spring-loaded contact in the field circuit
Contact opens above the setting, inserting a resistor; closes below it
Average field current set by duty cycle
Spring tension sets the voltage; three-unit regulator
Drawbacks: contact wear, arcing and radio noise, coarse regulation, adjustment
answer: Construction: an electromagnet (voltage coil) is connected across the generator output. Its armature carries a contact that sits in the field circuit and is held closed by a spring. A resistor is wired across the contact, so when the contact opens the resistor is put in series with the field winding.

Working: while the voltage is below the setting, the spring keeps the contact closed and full field current flows, so the voltage rises. When it passes the setting, the coil pulls the armature, the contact opens, the resistor enters the field circuit, the field current falls and the voltage falls. The coil then releases and the contact closes again. This repeats many times a second, and the voltage hovers round the setting. The spring tension sets the regulated voltage.
The average field current is set by the duty cycle D, the fraction of each cycle the contact is closed: I<sub>avg</sub> = D × I<sub>closed</sub> + (1 − D) × I<sub>open</sub>.

On light-aircraft DC generators it is built as a three-unit regulator: the voltage regulator, a current limiter (a second vibrating contact worked by a series coil that caps generator current) and a reverse-current cut-out that disconnects the generator when its voltage falls below the battery's.

Check: 0.357 × 3.50 + 0.643 × 1.167 = 1.250 + 0.750 = 2.00 A, as required. The field is inductive, so its current rises and falls along curves rather than jumping between 3.50 A and 1.167 A; the average-current method is the standard approximation.

Drawbacks: the contact makes and breaks field current, so it arcs; the arcing pits and wears the contact and radiates radio interference. Regulation is coarse because the contact can only switch between two levels, the spring and coil drift with temperature, and the regulator needs regular cleaning and adjustment. These are why carbon-pile and then electronic regulators replaced it.

bank.q: Explain the pitot-static system and how the airspeed indicator and the altimeter use it. At sea level q = 2500 Pa; find the indicated airspeed. With 1013.25 hPa set and 950 hPa outside, find the pressure altitude.
outline: Pitot senses total pressure P₀; static ports sense P
ASI capsule: P₀ inside, P outside, deflects with q
Calibrated at ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³; IAS, CAS, TAS
Altimeter: aneroid capsule on static only, subscale setting
Blockages: pitot (acts as altimeter), static (altimeter freezes)
answer: The pitot tube points into the airflow; its open end brings the air to rest, so it senses total pressure P₀. Static ports sit flush on the fuselage side, usually one on each side to cancel sideslip error, and sense the static pressure P. Each line has drains for water, and the pitot head is electrically heated against ice.

The airspeed indicator (ASI) has a capsule fed with P₀ inside, in a case fed with P. The capsule expands with the difference q = P₀ − P, and a linkage turns the needle. Below about Mach 0.3, q = ½ρV², and the dial is calibrated at sea-level density ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³. The reading is indicated airspeed (IAS); correcting for position error gives calibrated airspeed (CAS), and correcting CAS for density (and compressibility at high speed) gives true airspeed (TAS), which is higher than IAS at altitude.

The altimeter is a sealed aneroid capsule, nearly a vacuum inside, in a case fed with static pressure only. As the aircraft climbs, P falls, the capsule expands and the pointer turns. The subscale sets the reference pressure: QNH gives height above mean sea level near the airport, 1013.25 hPa gives pressure altitude (flight levels).

answer.pre:
difference = 1013.25 − 950 = 63.25 hPa
h ≈ 63.25 × 27 ft/hPa = 1707.8 ft, about 1710 ft

answer: Errors: position error from the airflow round the ports; lag; temperature error in the altimeter (in air colder than ISA the aircraft is lower than indicated).

Blockages: with the pitot blocked and its drain blocked, the trapped P₀ is fixed, so the ASI overreads in a climb and underreads in a descent, behaving like an altimeter. With the static blocked, the altimeter freezes, the VSI reads zero, and the ASI underreads in a climb and overreads in a descent; the alternate static source is selected.

Check: 124 kt is about Mach 0.19 at sea level, below Mach 0.3, so q = ½ρV² was valid. The 27 ft per hPa rule is a near-sea-level figure; at 950 hPa it is still close, so 1708 ft is a fair answer (the exact ISA value is about 1770 ft).

bank.q: An aircraft has a 115 V (line-to-neutral), 400 Hz three-phase main AC system. Explain how a transformer rectifier unit and a static inverter are used and why both are needed. A TRU of 90 % efficiency supplies 150 A at 28 V DC, and a static inverter of 85 % efficiency supplies a 500 VA standby AC bus at unity power factor from the 28 V DC bus. Find the TRU line current and the inverter's DC input current.
outline: TRU: three-phase transformer and diode bridge, AC to 28 V DC
Inverter: switching bridge and filter, DC to 115 V 400 Hz
Why both: normal DC from AC, standby AC from the battery
Use V<sub>LL</sub> = 200 V
TRU 13.5 A per line; inverter 21.0 A from the DC bus
answer: The TRU: a three-phase step-down transformer takes the 115/200 V AC bus down, and a full-wave diode bridge (often 12-pulse, from two secondaries 30° apart) turns it into 28 V DC with little ripple. It feeds the DC buses and charges the battery. TRUs of 100 to 200 A are common on transport aircraft.

The static inverter: a transistor bridge switches the 28 V DC on and off in a pattern, and a transformer and filter shape it into 115 V, 400 Hz sine-wave AC. Its frequency is set by the control oscillator, not by any shaft, so it stays at 400 Hz while the battery voltage falls. Older aircraft used rotary inverters (a DC motor turning an AC generator).

Why both are needed: in normal flight the AC generators carry everything, and the TRUs make the DC from AC, so the DC system needs no generator of its own. When all generators are lost, only DC (the battery) is left, but some essential instruments and avionics need AC; the inverter makes that AC from the battery-fed DC bus. So the TRU converts in the normal direction and the inverter in the emergency direction.

answer.text: TRU line current. Aircraft quote line-to-neutral voltage, so the line-to-line voltage is √3 × 115 = 199.2 V, about 200 V.

answer: Heat: the TRU turns 4666.7 − 4200 = 466.7 W into heat and the inverter 588.2 − 500 = 88.2 W, which the cooling system must remove.

Check: using 115 V instead of 200 V in √3 × V × I would give 23.4 A for the TRU, which is the common slip. Cross-check with phase quantities: 4666.7 ÷ (3 × 115) = 13.53 A, the same as 13.47 A within the rounding of 200 V. The inverter draws more current (21.0 A) than it delivers on the AC side (500 ÷ 115 = 4.35 A) because its input voltage is lower and it has losses.

bank.q: A 28 V DC load of 40 A is fed through an 8 m (one-way) feeder that passes a hot bay, where the wire must be derated to 70 % of its free-air rating. Explain how you would choose the wire and the protection device. The voltage drop must not exceed 2 % of 28 V; 8 AWG has 2.06 mΩ/m and 4 AWG has 0.815 mΩ/m.
outline: Free-air rating needed = 40 ÷ 0.7 = 57.1 A
Breaker at or below the derated wire rating, above the load
Time-current curve of the device below the wire damage curve
Voltage drop with the return path: 8 AWG 4.71 %, too much; 4 AWG 1.86 %
Check end-of-line fault and interrupting rating
answer: Start from the load, not the breaker: the wire must carry 40 A continuously in the hot bay, where it keeps only 70 % of its free-air rating. So the free-air rating needed is 40 ÷ 0.7 = 57.1 A. Choose a gauge whose table rating (for this insulation and bundle size) is at least 57.1 A; also apply any bundle and altitude factors the table gives.

Choose the breaker next. Its rating must be at least the load (40 A, so it does not nuisance-trip) and must not exceed the derated wire rating. If the chosen wire is rated 60 A in free air, its derated rating is 0.7 × 60 = 42 A, so a 40 A breaker fits between the 40 A load and the 42 A wire. A larger breaker would protect the load but not the wire.

Check the curves. On the time-current graph the breaker curve must lie below the wire damage curve at every fault current, so the breaker always opens before the insulation is damaged; and it must sit to the right of the load current, so it never opens in normal service.

answer.text: Check the voltage drop for 8 AWG (the return wire doubles the length).

answer: So the drop, not heating, sets the gauge here: 4 AWG is needed for the 2 % limit. A thicker wire has a higher current rating, so the breaker can stay at 40 A (sized for the load) with plenty of wire margin, or be chosen a step higher to avoid nuisance trips, as long as it stays below the thicker wire's derated rating.

Final checks: a short at the far end has the full loop resistance in series, so the fault current is lower and the breaker slower; confirm it still clears before the wire curve. Confirm the breaker is rated for DC and has enough interrupting capacity, because a DC arc does not go out at a current zero.

bank.q: Describe how the ram air turbine is deployed and what it feeds, and explain how ETOPS uses the available emergency power. An aircraft is approved for ETOPS 180 at 400 kt. Its RAT generator is rated 5 kVA and the emergency AC load is 3.2 kVA; the essential DC bus draws 1.4 kW at 28 V from a 23 Ah battery of which 50 % may be used. Find the ETOPS distance, the RAT loading and the battery time.
outline: Deployment on loss of all AC, automatic or manual
Feeds emergency AC bus; essential TRU makes essential DC
Battery bridges the seconds to RAT power
ETOPS: time to an alternate on one engine; third source (APU)
RAT airspeed band; load shedding
answer: Deployment: when all main AC power is lost, the RAT is released automatically (the crew can also release it); a small propeller on a strut swings into the airstream and spins up within seconds. A governor on the blade pitch holds its speed.

What it feeds: the RAT drives an emergency generator, directly or (on the A320) through the blue hydraulic system and a hydraulic motor. The generator feeds the emergency AC bus only, not the main buses. An essential TRU turns some of that AC into 28 V DC for the essential DC bus. Load shedding leaves only the flight instruments, one radio and navigation set, the flight controls and essential lighting.

The gap: in the seconds before the RAT is on line, the essential DC bus falls back to the battery through a contactor, and a static inverter can keep the AC standby bus alive. So the battery bridges, the RAT then carries the load, and the RAT must be kept inside its airspeed band.

ETOPS: Extended-range Twin-engine Operational Performance Standards limit how far, in one-engine-out flying time in still air, a twin may be from a suitable airport. For the electrical system, the remaining generator plus a third independent source (usually the APU generator, which must start at altitude after a cold soak) must carry the loads for the whole diversion; the RAT and battery cover only the case where all of those are lost.

head: Quantity
Working
Result
rows: Charge used in a 10 s bridge

answer: Interpret: the RAT has a 36 % margin, so it can carry the emergency loads with room for transients. The battery alone would last 13.8 minutes, far short of a 180-minute diversion, which is why the battery is only a bridge; bridging the few seconds before the RAT comes on line costs only about 0.14 Ah, about 1 % of the usable charge.
Check: 1200 nm at 400 kt is 3 h, the 180 minutes of the approval; 50 A × 0.23 h = 11.5 Ah, the usable charge. Both close.

bank.q: Explain how a tachometer and an EGT indicator turn engine speed and temperature into cockpit readings. An N1 pickup faces a 40-tooth wheel and 100 % N1 is 5000 rpm; find the pickup frequency at 92 % N1. A type K EGT thermocouple (41 µV/°C) has its hot junction at 760 °C and its cold junction at 40 °C; find the voltage and the reading an uncompensated indicator would give.
outline: Tacho-generator V = k × rpm, drag-cup, variable-reluctance pickup f = rpm ÷ 60 × N
Percent of a maker's reference speed
Thermocouple emf from T<sub>hot</sub> − T<sub>cold</sub>; probes in parallel
Cold-junction compensation and amplifier
3066.7 Hz; 29.52 mV; uncompensated reads 720 °C
answer: Speed sensing: a DC tacho-generator gives a voltage proportional to speed, V = k × rpm; a drag-cup indicator uses a magnet spun by a flexible shaft to drag a cup round against a hairspring; modern engines use a variable-reluctance pickup, a coil beside a toothed wheel, which gives one pulse per tooth. The pulse frequency is f = (rpm ÷ 60) × N, where N is the number of teeth, and the indicator or engine computer counts it.
The display shows percent of a reference speed chosen by the engine maker (N1 for the fan, N2 for the core), not rpm, so 92 % N1 and 92 % N2 are different speeds.

Temperature sensing: a type K (chromel-alumel) thermocouple produces an emf proportional to the difference between its hot junction in the exhaust and its cold junction at the instrument, V = S × (T<sub>hot</sub> − T<sub>cold</sub>). Several probes round the exhaust are wired in parallel, so the reading is their average. The cold junction is compensated (a circuit adds S × T<sub>cold</sub>), and the millivolt signal is amplified and converted to a reading in °C, with the limits marked in red.

answer.text: EGT voltage and the uncompensated reading.
answer.pre:
V = 41 µV/°C × (760 − 40) °C = 41 × 720 = 29 520 µV = 29.52 mV
an uncompensated indicator assumes T<sub>cold</sub> = 0 °C:
reading = 29 520 ÷ 41 = 720 °C   (40 °C low)

answer: Using the readings: at start the crew watches N2 rise and EGT peak and fall; an EGT above the start limit is a hot start and the start is abandoned. At take-off N1 sets thrust while EGT must stay below its red line, which on a hot day can limit thrust. A failed pickup gives no pulses (the reading drops to zero), and an open thermocouple gives a fixed low reading, so the two chains are monitored separately.

Check: the uncompensated error equals the cold-junction temperature, 40 °C, which is why compensation matters most when the instrument bay is warm. 3066.7 Hz ÷ 40 teeth × 60 = 4600 rpm, back to 92 % of 5000 rpm.

bank.q: Describe the packaging, cooling and EMI/EMC requirements for a line replaceable avionics unit, and name the standards used. An LRU dissipates 150 W into cooling air at 35 °C through a case-to-air resistance of 0.12 K/W; its case limit is 70 °C. Find the case temperature, and decide whether it still passes if a blocked filter doubles the resistance.
outline: LRU in a rack, front-loading, rear blind connector, hold-downs, keying
ARINC 404 (ATR sizes) and ARINC 600 (MCU sizes); military types
Forced air, cold plate or liquid; T<sub>case</sub> = T<sub>air</sub> + P × R<sub>th</sub>
EMI: suppress, route, filter, shield, bond; DO-160 and MIL-STD-461
53 °C passes; 71 °C fails by 1 K
answer: Packaging: an LRU is a sealed box that the line mechanic changes as one piece. It slides into a rack tray, a rear blind-mating connector engages as it is pushed home, hold-down clamps lock it against vibration, and keying pins stop a wrong box entering the tray. ARINC 404 sets air transport rack (ATR) case sizes, from ¼ ATR to 1 ATR; ARINC 600 sets the newer modular concept unit (MCU) sizes, connectors and cooling-air interface. Military boxes follow their own (DOD) standards with harsher shock, vibration and temperature limits.

Cooling: every watt lost raises temperature, and the limit is the hottest semiconductor junction. Small boxes cool by natural convection; larger ones by forced air blown through the case from the rack, by conduction to a cold plate, or by a liquid loop. One path is modelled by a thermal resistance: T<sub>case</sub> = T<sub>air</sub> + P × R<sub>th</sub>, then T<sub>j</sub> = T<sub>case</sub> + P<sub>device</sub> × R<sub>jc</sub> for each hot part. The installation must provide the airflow that the box was qualified with.

answer.pre:
rise  = 150 W × 0.12 K/W = 18 K
T<sub>case</sub> = 35 + 18 = 53 °C   (limit 70 °C: margin 17 K)

R<sub>th</sub> = 2 × 0.12 = 0.24 K/W
rise  = 150 × 0.24 = 36 K
T<sub>case</sub> = 35 + 36 = 71 °C   (1 K over the limit: fails)

answer: So a unit that passes on the bench can fail in the aircraft if its cooling air is restricted; maintenance must keep rack filters and fans serviceable, and the design margin should cover a credible loss of airflow.

EMI/EMC: the box must not emit more than the limits, conducted along its wires or radiated through space, and must keep working when exposed to the conducted and radiated levels of the aircraft (susceptibility). The controls work in layers: suppress at the source with filters and ferrites, route signal wires as screened twisted pairs away from power cables, filter every line at the connector with feed-through capacitors, shield the case with conductive gaskets, and bond the case to the airframe with a low-impedance strap. A poorly bonded shield is an antenna.

Standards: RTCA DO-160 covers the environmental and EMI tests of civil airborne equipment (temperature, altitude, vibration, power input, conducted and radiated emissions and susceptibility, lightning); MIL-STD-461 covers military EMI. Lightning and high-intensity radiated fields (HIRF) are checked as separate requirements.
Check: 35 + 150 × 0.12 = 53 °C and 35 + 150 × 0.24 = 71 °C; the 18 K rise doubles to 36 K when the resistance doubles, as it must for a linear model.

bank.q: Compare the A320 and B787 electrical architectures and evaluate why the B787 moved to 235 V AC variable frequency and ±270 V DC. Support the argument with the line current and copper loss of a 100 kW load at 115 V and at 235 V (line-to-neutral) through the same cable.
outline: A320: two 90 kVA IDGs, 115 V 400 Hz, APU 90 kVA, TRs 28 V DC, NiCd, RAT
B787: four 250 kVA VFSGs, 235 V 360-800 Hz, two 225 kVA APU SGs, ATRU ±270 V DC, Li-ion
Bleedless: electric pressurisation, anti-ice, start, brakes
Current halves, loss falls by 4.18
Gains: weight, no CSD, electric start; costs: VF loads, arcs, insulation, lithium
answer: A320 architecture: two IDGs, one per engine, each 90 kVA at 115/200 V, 400 Hz, each with its own GCU and line contactor onto AC BUS 1 or AC BUS 2; a bus tie contactor joins them when a generator is lost. The APU generator, also 90 kVA, can replace either IDG. Two 200 A transformer rectifiers make 28 V DC, an essential TR backs the essential DC bus, two NiCd batteries start the APU and bridge gaps, a static inverter makes essential AC from the battery, and the RAT drives a hydraulic emergency generator of about 5 kVA. Engine start, cabin pressure and wing anti-ice use bleed air.

B787 architecture: no engine bleed air, so pressurisation, wing ice protection, engine start, the brakes and some hydraulic pumps are electric. Each engine has two 250 kVA variable-frequency starter-generators (four in all) giving 235 V AC at about 360 to 800 Hz; two 225 kVA APU starter-generators add backup. ATRUs make ±270 V DC for large motor controllers, ATUs make 115 V AC, TRUs make 28 V DC, solid-state power controllers in remote power distribution units switch small loads, and lithium-ion batteries replace NiCd.

answer.text: Work the 100 kW comparison with phase voltages (aircraft voltages are line-to-neutral).

answer: Evaluate the voltage: the B787's main generators give 1000 kVA, more than five times the A320's 180 kVA (1450 kVA against 270 kVA with the APUs). At 115 V the currents, and so the copper weight or the loss, would be huge; at 235 V the current is about half and the loss for the same cable about a quarter, or the cable can be thinner for the same loss. ±270 V DC (540 V between the rails) does the same for the motor drives, and DC needs no frequency at all.

Evaluate the variable frequency: dropping the constant-speed drive removes a heavy, oil-cooled, high-maintenance gearbox from every generator, and the same machine can start the engine as a motor. The price is that every AC load must work over 360 to 800 Hz, so motors run through controllers and transformers are designed for the lowest frequency.

Evaluate the costs: higher voltages make arcs that do not self-extinguish (especially on DC), so the B787 needs arc-fault protection, solid-state switching, better insulation and connectors; partial discharge must be considered at altitude. Lithium-ion batteries save weight but brought the 2013 thermal-runaway grounding and a containment redesign.

Verdict: for an aircraft that must make megawatts of electric power because it has no bleed air, higher voltage and variable frequency are the lighter and more efficient choice; for the A320, with its bleed-air systems and smaller electrical load, the mature 115 V 400 Hz system is adequate. Check: 3 × 115 × 289.9 = 100 000 W and 3 × 235 × 141.8 = 100 000 W.

bank.q: Explain split, parallel and split-parallel bus systems and analyse what happens in each when one generator fails in flight. Two 28 V DC generators rated 200 A each carry bus loads of 150 A and 130 A. Each has a no-load voltage of 28.5 V; generator 1 droops 0.4 V per 100 A and generator 2 0.6 V per 100 A. Find the sharing when paralleled and the load to shed after one fails.
outline: Split: each generator its own bus; fault contained; lost generator strands its bus
Parallel: one bus; synchronising and load sharing by droop; one fault can pull down all
Split-parallel: split normally, BTB closes on failure after load shedding
Droop sharing I₁ = 168 A, I₂ = 112 A at 27.83 V
After failure: 280 A on 200 A, shed at least 80 A
answer: Split (isolated) bus: each generator feeds its own bus through its own GCB and the buses are never joined. A fault on bus 1 trips only GCB 1. If generator 1 fails, bus 1 is stranded: its DC loads can be carried by the battery or a TRU from the other side, but whatever is left on bus 1 alone is lost. No synchronising is needed because two generators never share a bar.

Parallel bus: all generators close onto one bus and share the load. AC machines must be synchronised (voltage, frequency, phase) before closing; sharing is set by droop and load controllers. If one generator fails, the others carry the whole load at once with no break, but a fault on the common bus, or a generator fault that its protection misses, can pull every generator down together.

answer.text: Load sharing in parallel (equal no-load voltages).

answer: So the stiffer machine (generator 1) carries more: 168 A against 112 A, both under their 200 A ratings. A load controller would trim the fields to bring them nearer 140 A each.

Split-parallel bus: the normal state of most twin transports. In normal flight the bus tie breaker (BTB) is open, so the system behaves as split, with fault containment and no sharing problem: generator 1 carries 150 A and generator 2 carries 130 A. When a generator fails, its GCB opens and the BTB closes, so the survivor feeds both buses, giving the redundancy of a parallel system.

answer.pre:
load on the survivor = 150 + 130 = 280 A
rating = 200 A  →  shed at least 280 − 200 = 80 A
(shedding galleys and cabin loads first)

answer.text: Compare the three on a single failure.

head: Layout
Fault on one bus
One generator fails
rows: Its bus stranded (battery or TRU for DC only)
No break; survivor must carry 280 A
BTB closes after 80 A is shed

answer: Conclusion: split-parallel joins the fault containment of split operation with the redundancy of parallel operation, at the cost of the BTB logic and load shedding. Check: 168 + 112 = 280 A, and both generators sit at 27.83 V.

bank.q: Fuel quantity is often called the hardest cockpit measurement. Analyse why, and evaluate the correction methods used. A capacitance probe reads 35.4 pF empty and 70.8 pF full; and 10 000 litres of fuel at 0.80 kg/L is shown with a stale density of 0.78 kg/L: find the probe reading at half height and the mass error.
outline: Tank shape, attitude, slosh and acceleration
Capacitance follows wetted height; εr changes with fuel type and temperature
Density turns volume into mass
Compensator, densitometer, multiple probes and tank tables
Flow-integration cross-check and dripsticks
answer: Why it is hard: the fuel lies in irregular wing tanks that flex, pitch, roll and accelerate, so the surface tilts and the local level at any one probe is not the true quantity; the fuel's dielectric constant and density change with fuel type and temperature; and the crew wants mass (kilograms, for range and weight) while the sensors see height or volume.

The capacitance probe: two concentric tubes form a capacitor; fuel (εr about 2.0) rising between them replaces air (εr = 1.0), so C = C<sub>empty</sub> + (C<sub>full</sub> − C<sub>empty</sub>) × h ÷ H. It has no moving parts, unlike a float and rheostat, which can stick and gives only one point per tank.
Correction 1, the dielectric: a compensator probe at the bottom of the tank is always fully wet and measures the fuel's own εr, so the bridge reads height correctly whatever the fuel.

Correction 2, the density: mass = volume × density. A densitometer in the tank, or a density figure from refuelling, converts volume to mass. A wrong density gives a wrong mass even when the volume is right:

answer.text: Mass error from a stale density.
answer.pre:
true mass  = 10 000 L × 0.80 kg/L = 8000 kg
shown mass = 10 000 L × 0.78 kg/L = 7800 kg
error = 200 kg = 200 ÷ 8000 × 100 = 2.5 % (under-reading)

answer: Correction 3, attitude and shape: many probes per tank, spread out, plus a tank table that turns the set of probe heights into volume for the current pitch and roll; the fuel computer averages them and flags a disagreement.

Cross-checks: fuel used from integrated fuel flow is subtracted from the start quantity and compared with the gauges; a gauge falling faster than the burn points to a leak or a probe or density fault. On the ground, dripsticks (magnetic level indicators) give an independent reading.

Evaluation: the compensator removes the εr error and the multi-probe tank tables remove most of the attitude error, so the remaining weak point is density, a 2.5 % error in this example; that is why modern systems measure density in the tank rather than take a figure from the paperwork. Check: 53.1 pF is midway between 35.4 and 70.8 pF, as a half-full parallel-plate probe must be.

bank.q: Evaluate the consequences of fitting a circuit breaker larger than the wire's derated rating, and explain the role of current limiters and limiting resistors. Use a wire rated 25 A whose damage time is t = 30 000 ÷ (I² − 625) s, the 20 A breaker t = 6000 ÷ (I² − 400) s and a 50 A breaker t = 37 500 ÷ (I² − 2500) s, all at a 60 A fault. A limiting resistor of 0.5 Ω is put in series with a 28 V load: what is the largest inrush current?
outline: Oversized breaker: wire becomes the fuse, insulation chars, fire risk
At 60 A: wire 10.1 s, 20 A breaker 1.9 s, 50 A breaker 34.1 s
Below 50 A the large breaker never trips: sustained overload
Current limiter: slow-blow heavy-current fuse on feeders
Limiting resistor: 28 ÷ 0.5 = 56 A inrush cap
Undersizing also fails: nuisance trips
answer: The rule: a breaker protects the wire, not the load. Its curve must lie below the wire damage curve at every current, and its rating must not exceed the wire's derated rating.

answer.text: Compare the times at a 60 A fault.

answer: With the 20 A breaker the fault clears in 1.9 s, well before the wire's 10.1 s: correct. With the 50 A breaker the wire is damaged at 10.1 s while the breaker would not open until 34.1 s, so the wire itself becomes the fuse: the insulation softens and chars, smoke and toxic fumes form in the bundle, neighbouring wires can be damaged, and an arc can start a fire.

Worse, between 25 A and 50 A the 50 A breaker never trips at all, so a sustained overload of, say, 40 A cooks the wire indefinitely without any trip; this is the most dangerous case because nothing tells the crew.

Current limiters: a current limiter is a heavy-current, slow-blow fuse used on generator and main feeders and bus ties. It carries large short overloads (motor starts) but melts on a sustained fault, so it isolates a faulted feeder before the main busbar sees the full fault current. It is not resettable and must be coordinated so the load breakers downstream clear local faults first.

answer.pre:
largest inrush = V ÷ R = 28 V ÷ 0.5 Ω = 56 A
(the load's own resistance would lower it further)

answer: A limiting resistor is put in series to hold down the inrush of a capacitive or motor load, or the fault current of a circuit, to a value a smaller breaker or contactor can handle; it limits, it does not break the circuit, and it is often bypassed by a contactor once the load is up to speed.

Evaluation: oversizing a breaker removes the wire's protection and is a fire risk; undersizing it (below the load current) causes nuisance trips and repeated resets, which also heat the wire. The right breaker sits between the load current and the derated wire rating. Check: 30 000 ÷ 2975 = 10.08 s, 6000 ÷ 3200 = 1.875 s, 37 500 ÷ 1100 = 34.09 s.

glossary.def: Auxiliary power unit: a small gas turbine in the tail that supplies electrical and pneumatic power on the ground and in flight if needed.
Integrated drive generator: an engine-driven generator with a built-in constant-speed drive so it always produces 400 Hz AC.
A heavy-duty relay that makes and breaks a main power circuit under control of a switch or protection relay.
A contactor that joins two busbars, either to share load between generators or to let one generator feed both sides.
Circuit of diodes that converts alternating current into direct current.
The pressure produced by motion, equal to half the density times the square of the speed, written ½ρV².
The pressure of still air at the aircraft's altitude, sensed by ports on the fuselage side.
Junction of two unlike metals that produces a small voltage proportional to the temperature difference between its hot and cold ends.
Correction applied for the temperature of the thermocouple's reference end, so the reading is the hot-end temperature only.
The small DC current fed to a generator's field winding, which sets the strength of the magnetic field and hence the output voltage.
Supplying the field current; a generator with no excitation produces no output.
Automatically removing non-essential loads so a reduced power source can keep the essential ones running.
A busbar reserved for loads that must keep running: flight instruments, radios, flight controls, and minimum lighting.
Reducing a component's allowed current below its catalogue value to allow for high ambient temperature, altitude, or tightly bundled wires.
Resettable protection device that opens on overcurrent and can be reset by the crew after a fault is cleared.
Slow-acting protective device for heavy feeder circuits; carries normal current indefinitely but opens on a large sustained fault.
External cart or pit supply that feeds the aircraft busbars while the engines and APU are off.
High-intensity radiated fields: strong external radio or radar energy the aircraft's wiring must not pick up as a false signal.
Fuel tank sensor whose capacitance changes as fuel rises between its plates; used to infer fuel level.
Flashing red beacon that warns ground crew and other traffic that the aircraft is about to move or is running.
Forward-facing open tube on the fuselage that senses total pressure for the airspeed indicator.
Instrument that displays engine shaft speed, usually as a percentage of the maximum rated speed.
Transformer rectifier unit; steps AC down and rectifies it to DC, typically giving 28 V DC from 115 V AC.
Built-in test equipment: self-check circuits inside a unit that report faults to the cockpit or a maintenance panel.
Auto-transformer rectifier unit: an auto-transformer with a multi-pulse rectifier that turns 235 V AC into ±270 V DC on the B787.
The electronics in a lithium-ion battery that watch each cell's voltage and temperature, balance the cells and stop charging when a limit is reached.
Generator circuit breaker: the heavy-duty contactor, commanded by the GCU, that connects a generator to its bus; Airbus calls it the generator line contactor.
The fall of a generator's terminal voltage as its current rises, V = V₀ − kI; it sets how paralleled generators share load.
